title: A Will Probated in 1992 Still Governs the Property, Madras High Court Tells MGR's Brother's Heirs in 2026
meta_description: Madras High Court rejects a Letters of Administration claim by MGR's brother's heirs, holding MGR's probated 1987 will already covers the property.
citation: O.P. No. 69 of 2012, with connected A.Nos. 3416, 3417, 3419 of 2026 & 4268 of 2023, Madras High Court, decided 24 September 2026
body: A property dispute tied to the estate of former Tamil Nadu Chief Minister M.G. Ramachandran has been running in one form or another since the 1990s, and the Madras High Court has just closed one more front of it. Heirs of MGR's brother, M.G. Chakrapani, had sought Letters of Administration over a property in Virugambakkam, Chennai, arguing that MGR had died intestate as to this particular asset. Justice A.D. Maria Clete rejected that claim outright.

The petition was old even by the standards of estate litigation. O.P. No. 69 of 2012 had sat on the Original Side docket for well over a decade, with connected applications, A.Nos. 3416, 3417 and 3419 of 2026 along with A.No. 4268 of 2023, filed along the way as the Chakrapani heirs pressed their claim. Their theory was narrow but, if accepted, would have reopened a slice of MGR's estate that everyone else had treated as settled for more than thirty years: they argued that because MGR's will did not specifically dispose of the Virugambakkam property, he had died intestate as to that asset, and intestate succession should apply to it instead.

The court's answer turned on a document that was never really in dispute: MGR's will, dated 18 January 1987. That will had already been probated by the Madras High Court itself, back in 1992. Justice Clete held that the Virugambakkam property was in fact covered by the terms of that 1987 will, which meant there was no gap in the testamentary disposition for intestate succession to fill. The probate granted decades earlier was not something the Chakrapani heirs could get around simply by arguing, now, that one particular property had somehow been left out of it.

That finding did the real work in the case. Once the court held the property fell within the probated will's scope, the entire premise of the Letters of Administration petition collapsed, because such letters are granted precisely to administer property an intestate person left behind, not property already disposed of by a will that has stood probated and unchallenged for over three decades.

The ruling is a useful marker for how long a testamentary dispute can be kept alive through incremental applications, and for how little traction a late-stage intestacy argument gets once a will has actually been probated. Probate is not a formality that a disappointed heir can quietly route around years later by picking out one asset and arguing it fell through a gap in the document. If the property is covered by the will's terms, the probate order answers the intestacy question definitively, and a court is not going to reopen that question property by property on an heir's say-so.

For estate practitioners, the case is also a reminder of how family succession disputes involving a public figure's estate tend to generate satellite litigation for generations after the original testator's death. MGR died in December 1987, and in 2026 the Madras High Court is still disposing of petitions filed by relatives probing for assets the probated will might have missed. Clients advising such heirs would do well to test, early and rigorously, whether the specific property they are chasing is actually covered by the probated will's language before investing years in litigation premised on an intestacy that the document itself forecloses.

The length of time involved also says something about how estate disputes of this kind actually unfold in practice. A petition filed in 2012 was still generating fresh interlocutory applications fourteen years later, each one adding delay and cost without disturbing the basic legal question the probated will had already answered back in 1992. Respondents facing a similar pattern of repeated applications built around the same underlying asset would do well to point the court, as happened here, to the probate order itself as the shortest route to disposing of the whole string of filings at once, rather than contesting each application on its own narrower terms.
why_it_matters: Heirs considering a Letters of Administration petition against an estate that has already been through probate should first establish, with real certainty, that the specific asset they are chasing falls outside the probated will's terms. This ruling confirms that an Indian court will not revisit a decades-old probate order property by property simply because a later claimant argues the will left a particular asset undisposed.
card_summary: Madras High Court rejects a Letters of Administration petition by MGR's brother's heirs, holding MGR's 1987 will, probated in 1992, already covers the asset and leaves no room for intestacy.
card_tip: Before filing a Letters of Administration petition against a probated estate, confirm the asset actually falls outside the will's terms; probate forecloses intestacy claims asset by asset.
verification_notes: Confirmed via two independent reports, Bar and Bench (24 September 2026) and SupremeToday.ai, both describing the same Madras High Court ruling by Justice A.D. Maria Clete rejecting a Letters of Administration petition by M.G. Chakrapani's heirs over the Virugambakkam property, on the ground that MGR's will of 18 January 1987, probated in 1992, already covered that property. The case name 'Ramamurthy v. Rajendran' is inferred from the filename of the judgment PDF hosted by Bar and Bench alongside its report (images.assettype.com/barandbench/2026-09-26/.../Ramamurthy_Vs_Rajendran.pdf) and was not confirmed by independently reading the order text, so it should be verified against the order itself before publication if a higher degree of certainty is required. The case numbers (O.P. No. 69 of 2012 and the connected A.Nos.) and the probate and will dates are drawn from the two reports cited.
